name: Extract Function

human.symptom: A function body that needs a mental outline before you can read it — multiple concerns interleaved, or chunks of statements that share a single domain purpose without a name.
human.goal: Each function reads as a single named domain step — what it does, not how.
human.pressure: Every reader pays the outline cost on every read; small edits to one concern require holding all the others in working memory; PRs touch the same function for unrelated reasons.
human.tradeoff: Over-eager extraction can produce a maze of one-line functions; aim for extractions that earn their name with at least one decision or one transformation.
human.relief: Calling code becomes a sequence of named intentions; bugs concentrate inside the now-named subroutines.
human.trap: A maze of one-line helpers where the workflow can no longer be read linearly — extraction that doesn't earn its name fragments the procedure into pieces too small to mean anything.

agent.symptom: A function whose token count exceeds the agent's reliable chunk-reasoning budget; verifying behavior preservation requires re-reading the entire span on every edit.
agent.goal: Each function is a verifiable unit small enough that the agent can reason about its full behavior in a single reasoning step.
agent.pressure: Every edit pays full re-read cost; chained changes compound context usage and increase the chance of missing a cross-statement invariant.
agent.tradeoff: Each extracted helper inflates context-window cost by one definition the next reasoning step must load; over-extracting blows effective working memory.
agent.relief: Smaller diff surface per commit; behavior preservation verifiable per refactoring step; chained orchestrations work from named subroutines instead of re-derived semantics.
agent.trap: Forces the agent to chase a dozen function definitions to follow what was once a 20-line procedure — context cost inflates and cross-function invariants disappear.

name: Inline Function

human.symptom: A function whose name is no clearer than its body — wrappers that add no semantic value (`moreThanFive(n) { return n > 5 }`), pass-through functions called only once, or thin abstractions over trivial expressions.
human.goal: Trivial wrappers vanish; the call site reads as exactly what's happening.
human.pressure: Readers pay a hop to look up the wrapper only to find it adds nothing; the indirection crowds the file with definitions that don't earn their keep.
human.tradeoff: If the function had a meaningful name covering several call sites, inlining can scatter the intent — only inline when the body is as clear as the wrapper.
human.relief: One fewer indirection to follow when reading; smaller surface to maintain.
human.trap: Inlining wrappers that genuinely add meaning — `isOverdue(invoice)` is clearer than `invoice.dueDate < today()` even if mechanically identical — strips the named domain concept.

agent.symptom: A function whose body the agent must trace through only to find no decisions or transformations — every reference site pays a context-load hop for no reasoning gain.
agent.goal: Trivial wrappers disappear from the agent's working context; call sites read as exactly what's happening.
agent.pressure: The agent loads the wrapper definition to verify any change touching it; the indirection is a tax on every reasoning step.
agent.tradeoff: Inlining scatters the wrapper's body across call sites; if the wrapper was a seam (mocking boundary, extension point), removing it forecloses options the agent might need later.
agent.relief: Shorter call chains; the agent loads one fewer definition per reasoning step.
agent.trap: Mechanically inlining every short function — including ones that name a real domain concept — collapses semantic anchors the agent uses to reason about behavior.

name: Extract Variable
before: if (order.qty * order.price - Math.max(0, order.qty - 500) * order.price * 0.05 > 1000) { /* ... */ }

human.symptom: A long expression in a conditional, return statement, or method argument that the reader must mentally parse — multiple operations on multiple inputs producing one value.
human.goal: A complex expression earns a name that says what it represents in the domain.
human.pressure: Readers pay parsing cost every time; debugging the value requires breakpoints inside the expression; comments scatter to explain what subexpressions mean.
human.tradeoff: Over-extracting tiny expressions clutters scope with one-shot names; extract when the expression carries domain meaning the surrounding code can't speak.
human.relief: Reusable in nearby code; debugging shows the intermediate value; comments explaining the expression become unnecessary.
human.trap: Extracting every short expression — including ones already self-explanatory — clutters scope with one-shot names that obscure rather than reveal intent.

agent.symptom: An expression complex enough that the agent must parse it sub-step by sub-step to interpret; subsequent reasoning about the value requires re-parsing the full expression.
agent.goal: Intermediate values have names the agent can reference directly; reasoning about the expression decomposes into reasoning about named sub-values.
agent.pressure: The agent re-parses complex expressions at every reference; debugging requires the agent to mentally evaluate the full subexpression chain.
agent.tradeoff: Each extracted variable is a name in the agent's local scope; over-extraction creates scope clutter the agent must navigate to find what's actually relevant.
agent.relief: The agent references named intermediate values; expression-level reasoning becomes reference-level reasoning, which is cheaper.
agent.trap: Extracting every sub-expression — including ones already obvious — bloats the agent's scope table with names that document nothing the agent didn't already know.

name: Inline Variable
before:
const basePrice = order.basePrice;
return basePrice > 1000;
after: return order.basePrice > 1000;

human.symptom: A local variable that's just a rename of its right-hand side — `const basePrice = order.basePrice;` — adding no domain meaning the original expression didn't already carry.
human.goal: Single-use variables that just rename their right-hand side disappear; the expression speaks for itself.
human.pressure: Readers track an extra name for nothing; small scopes balloon with redundant references; the variable's existence implies meaning it doesn't have.
human.tradeoff: Inlining a name that did carry domain meaning costs readability — only inline when the expression is already self-explanatory.
human.relief: Less local clutter, fewer redundant names, smaller scopes to track.
human.trap: Inlining a variable whose name did carry domain meaning — collapsing `const annualRate = 0.05` to bare `0.05` strips the named constant the reader needed.

agent.symptom: A local variable whose name says the same thing as the expression bound to it; reading the variable name and reading the expression resolve to the same understanding.
agent.goal: Expressions sit at their use sites without an intervening binding; the agent reads the expression once at the use site instead of reading the variable name plus the binding's definition.
agent.pressure: The agent tracks an extra name in scope for no reasoning benefit; reference resolution becomes a tiny hop to a definition that adds nothing.
agent.tradeoff: Inlining a variable that did carry domain meaning forces the agent to interpret the bare expression every time instead of reading the named concept.
agent.relief: One fewer name in scope to resolve at every read; the agent loads the expression once at its single use site instead of paying the lookup hop from the variable to its definition.
agent.trap: Inlining a variable whose name carried a non-obvious meaning (a domain term, an intermediate result) forces the agent to re-derive the meaning of the expression at every site it appears, multiplying token cost across uses.

name: Change Function Declaration

human.symptom: A function whose name doesn't match what it does, or whose parameter list carries unused/awkwardly-ordered arguments — readers must inspect the body to understand the call.
human.goal: Function names match what they actually do; parameter lists carry only what the function needs, in the order callers expect.
human.pressure: Every reader of a call site pays a comprehension cost; mismatches between name and behavior hide bugs; new callers learn the wrong abstraction from the wrong signature.
human.tradeoff: Every caller pays for the signature change at once, even those whose call sites were already fine; other-team callers get forced coordination.
human.relief: Call sites read fluently; mismatches between expectation and behavior surface immediately at the boundary.
human.trap: Renaming or reshaping signatures across team boundaries without coordination — forces other teams to rebuild their code in your PR's timeline.

agent.symptom: A function whose name or signature doesn't match its behavior; the agent inferring intent from the call site gets misled and must read the body to verify.
agent.goal: Names and signatures express what the function does; the agent reasons about call sites from the signature alone.
agent.pressure: The agent must read the function body to verify call-site intent; chained edits compound the cost as the agent re-derives intent at every site.
agent.tradeoff: Every caller pays for the change at once; for cross-team consumers, the agent must coordinate updates or risk breaking external code.
agent.relief: Call sites read fluently; the agent's signature-based reasoning becomes trustworthy; mismatches surface at the boundary.
agent.trap: Reshaping signatures across team boundaries without coordination forces other consumers to rebuild — the agent shipping the change may not see the downstream breakage.

name: Encapsulate Variable
before: let defaultOwner = { firstName: 'Martin', lastName: 'Fowler' };

human.symptom: A module-level variable or shared mutable state read and written directly from any consumer — no central audit point for changes.
human.goal: All reads and writes pass through a small named function that owns validation, logging, and invariants.
human.pressure: Adding validation, logging, or invariant checks requires touching every consumer; bugs from concurrent mutation hide in the gaps; the variable's lifetime is implicit.
human.tradeoff: Adds a layer of indirection that pays off only when every access goes through the wrapper — leakage of direct access undoes the benefit.
human.relief: A bug fix or audit becomes a one-line addition inside the wrapper; consumers never need to change.
human.trap: Adding a getter/setter wrapper without removing the direct access — adds indirection ceremony while consumers still bypass the wrapper, so the encapsulation provides no real guarantee.

agent.symptom: The agent finds a variable read and written from multiple consumers with no central function owning the access; reasoning about any read requires modeling every writer.
agent.goal: All access goes through a small named function the agent can grep for, audit, and instrument as a single closed surface.
agent.pressure: Any change to validation, logging, or invariants requires the agent to update every consumer; concurrent edits compound the search-and-update cost.
agent.tradeoff: Indirection at every call site adds a hop; if any consumer leaks past the wrapper, the encapsulation's safety promise silently breaks and the agent assumes guarantees that don't hold.
agent.relief: The agent has one audit point for validation/logging/invariants; consumers don't need to change when the wrapper grows new behavior.
agent.trap: Wrapping the variable without enforcing wrapper-only access leaves leaks the agent doesn't see; the wrapper becomes a false safety signal.

name: Rename Variable
before: const a = height * width;
after: const area = height * width;

human.symptom: A variable named `t`, `temp`, `data`, `result`, or any other identifier that requires the reader to inspect its assignment to know what it holds.
human.goal: Variable names match the domain role they play, not their implementation type or scratch nature.
human.pressure: Every reader pays a re-comprehension cost when they encounter the variable; bugs hide in the gap between what the name suggests and what the code does.
human.tradeoff: The IDE renames code, not the world around it — cross-repo greps, commit history, comments, and string-literal references silently drift stale.
human.relief: Reading the variable's name tells you everything you need without checking its definition.
human.trap: Renaming bikeshedding — endless rename churn for marginal clarity gains while the actual code structure stays unimproved.

agent.symptom: The agent encounters a variable whose identifier doesn't disambiguate scope or domain; reasoning about any expression involving the variable requires loading the surrounding context first.
agent.goal: Variable names carry enough disambiguating information that the agent can reason about each symbol without a lookup hop.
agent.pressure: Every reasoning pass re-derives meaning from surrounding context; chained edits compound the cost.
agent.tradeoff: Renames invalidate cached associations — commit history, RAG snippets, embedding indexes, and prior conversation context all carry the old name until they refresh.
agent.relief: Per-occurrence reading cost drops to one token of name; reasoning steps that previously had to load surrounding scope to interpret the symbol now resolve from the name alone.
agent.trap: Renaming variables whose current names another reviewer would have accepted invalidates cached associations (RAG indexes, prior conversation context, comments) without changing what the symbol represents.

name: Introduce Parameter Object
before:
function recordTemperature(low, high, value) { /* ... */ }
function alertIfOutOfRange(low, high, reading) { /* ... */ }

human.symptom: The same group of fields (low, high; firstName, lastName; street, city, zip) appears as parameters across multiple functions — a clump traveling together with no name.
human.goal: Related arguments travel together as one well-named value object that the function (and callers) refer to by name.
human.pressure: Adding a field of the clump touches every signature; callers must remember positional order; the clump's identity stays invisible.
human.tradeoff: Premature parameter objects hide which fields are actually needed by which method — wait until the clump appears in 3+ places before extracting.
human.relief: Adding a related field is one type change instead of touching every call site; intent is named.
human.trap: Building parameter objects from coincidental groupings (params that happen to appear together but don't share a domain concept) — adds a class for ceremony without expressing meaning.

agent.symptom: The agent sees the same field group appearing across multiple signatures; every site re-parses the same shape and verifies the same ordering.
agent.goal: The clump becomes a named value object the agent passes through as a single token; structure validation happens once at construction.
agent.pressure: Adding or reordering a field touches every signature; the agent must find and update each consistently or risk silent positional drift.
agent.tradeoff: Constructing the object at every call adds an allocation and a name the agent must learn; if the clump appears in <3 places the wrapper is overhead.
agent.relief: Operations on the clump (formatting, validation, equality) live with it; the agent reasons about one named concept instead of N coupled fields.
agent.trap: Wrapping coincidental field groups creates fake value objects the agent must construct and destructure with no comprehension gain.

name: Combine Functions into Class

human.symptom: Two or more functions all take the same data shape as their first parameter and operate on its fields — passive data being acted on from outside.
human.goal: Functions that all act on the same data live alongside it as methods; calls become method calls on a domain object.
human.pressure: The data's invariants aren't enforced anywhere; logic that belongs together scatters across modules; new operations have to re-import the data shape and re-derive its rules.
human.tradeoff: Wrapping passive data in a class that nobody else uses adds ceremony — only combine when 2+ functions take the same data and would benefit from co-located behavior.
human.relief: Encapsulation tightens; tests target the class; new operations land in one obvious place.
human.trap: Wrapping passive data in a class that nobody else needs to be a class — adds construction ceremony at every entry point with no encapsulation gain.

agent.symptom: The agent finds multiple functions that all take the same data shape; reasoning about the data requires loading every operation that touches it scattered across files.
agent.goal: Operations live with the data they act on; the agent loads one class to reason about both shape and behavior.
agent.pressure: The agent traces operations across modules to understand what the data can do; invariants the agent must respect aren't enforced at construction.
agent.tradeoff: Wrapping the data in a class adds construction ceremony at every entry point; for data only used in one place the class is more code than the original concern warranted.
agent.relief: The agent loads the class as a single unit; behavior, fields, and invariants all in one place with one import.
agent.trap: Wrapping data that nobody else operates on creates a class the agent must instantiate everywhere with no encapsulation gain — pure overhead.

name: Combine Functions into Transform

human.symptom: Multiple consumers compute the same derived values from the same source data, each independently re-deriving the result.
human.goal: Multiple derived values from the same source come from one transform that produces an enriched record.
human.pressure: Derivations drift between consumers as they age; bugs hide where two consumers compute slightly different versions; performance suffers from redundant computation.
human.tradeoff: Building a transform up-front when only one derivation exists is BDUF — wait for the second derivation before introducing the transform.
human.relief: Derivations stay consistent (no two callers compute slightly different versions); cache invalidation becomes obvious.
human.trap: Building a transform up-front when only one consumer derives anything — BDUF abstraction that adds an intermediate type without an active second user.

agent.symptom: The agent encounters consumers each independently computing the same derived values from the same source; reasoning about consistency requires tracing every derivation.
agent.goal: One transform produces the enriched record; the agent reasons about derivations in one place and consumers read named fields.
agent.pressure: Each consumer re-derives the same values; the agent can't trust them to be consistent and must verify equivalence on every change.
agent.tradeoff: Building the transform when only one consumer exists creates an intermediate type the agent must learn before its second use justifies it.
agent.relief: Derivations are consistent by construction; the agent reads field accesses on the enriched record instead of computing across the codebase.
agent.trap: Pre-building transforms for hypothetical consumers creates intermediate shapes the agent must understand and maintain with no active reuse.

name: Split Phase

human.symptom: A function that mixes two clearly different concerns — pricing AND rendering, parsing AND validating, fetching AND transforming — interleaved through shared locals.
human.goal: Each phase reads and writes its own well-defined inputs and outputs; the seam between them is data, not control flow.
human.pressure: Each concern can't be tested or evolved independently; changes to one concern risk breaking the other; the function's intent gets buried under coordination work.
human.tradeoff: An intermediate data structure between the phases is overhead — earn it by separating two clearly different concerns.
human.relief: Phases evolve independently; tests target each phase in isolation; the intermediate shape becomes a documented contract.
human.trap: Splitting phases that genuinely belong together — work where the second phase needs to mutate state the first phase set up in subtle ways — fragments coherent logic across an artificial seam.

agent.symptom: The agent finds a function that conflates two concerns in interleaved code; reasoning about either concern requires tracing through the other.
agent.goal: Each phase reads and writes its own well-defined inputs and outputs; the agent reasons about phases independently with the intermediate shape as the contract.
agent.pressure: The agent must trace interleaved concerns through one function body; testing or modifying either requires reasoning about both.
agent.tradeoff: The intermediate data structure is overhead; for functions where the two phases are tightly coupled (shared mutable locals, observer effects), splitting adds a seam without buying isolation.
agent.relief: Each phase becomes the agent's unit of reasoning; the intermediate shape documents the contract; testing and modification isolate to one phase at a time.
agent.trap: Splitting tightly-coupled phases creates an artificial seam the agent must coordinate across — the intermediate shape leaks one phase's implementation into the next.

name: Move Function

human.symptom: A function on class A that reads only data on class B — A.method() reaches through getters on B to compute something B should compute.
human.goal: Each function lives where its data lives; coupling between modules drops.
human.pressure: B's internals leak through public surfaces just to support A's method; refactoring B becomes a coordination across A's call sites.
human.tradeoff: Dependencies don't always travel cleanly — circular imports surface at the destination, and readers' 'where does this live' map briefly breaks.
human.relief: Modules become more cohesive; tests stay focused; feature-envy patterns disappear.
human.trap: Moving every cross-class read mechanically — including functions that legitimately compose data across multiple classes — fan-outs the move and breaks coherent abstractions.

agent.symptom: A function's body references foreign-class data more than its own; the agent loading the function must also load the foreign class to verify any change.
agent.goal: Each function lives where its data lives; the agent loads one class to reason about one behavior.
agent.pressure: Each call to the envious function pulls a second class into the agent's working context; chained reasoning across the boundary compounds the load.
agent.tradeoff: Dependencies don't always travel cleanly — circular imports surface at the destination, and the agent's mental map of 'where does this live' briefly breaks until indices refresh.
agent.relief: The function's data sits inside the agent's current reasoning context; verifying behavior touches one class instead of two.
agent.trap: Mechanical move-the-function-to-the-data on every cross-class read creates a fan-out the agent must follow at every call site — the cure becomes a worse smell than the original.

name: Move Field

human.symptom: A field on class A whose value is determined by data on class B (`customer.discountRate` set from `customer.plan.kind`) — the field belongs with the data it's derived from.
human.goal: Each field belongs to the class that owns its lifecycle; cross-class reaching disappears.
human.pressure: Every consumer of A must maintain the cross-class invariant; refactoring B's data shape breaks A in non-obvious ways; the field's true owner is invisible.
human.tradeoff: Every reader of the original class now reaches across the new class boundary — coupling drops at the field's new home but reappears at each consumer.
human.relief: Class boundaries align with data ownership; mutations are local; refactoring becomes safer.
human.trap: Moving fields whose presence on the original class is part of the class's identity — even when the value derives elsewhere, moving the field can break consumer expectations.

agent.symptom: The agent finds a field on class A whose value is determined by data on class B; reasoning about the field's value requires loading B to verify the derivation.
agent.goal: Each field lives in the class that determines its value; reading the field and reading the data that determines it happen in the same class file.
agent.pressure: Every consumer must maintain the cross-class invariant; the agent verifying any change must coordinate updates across both classes.
agent.tradeoff: Every previous reader of the field now loads the new owner class to read it; tokens that previously stayed in one file now span two, and the agent follows the new boundary at every read site.
agent.relief: Mutations to the field stay inside the class that determines its value; the agent reads one class file to predict both the field's value and the data that drives it.
agent.trap: Moving fields purely on derivation grounds — without checking whether the original class's identity depends on the field's presence — breaks consumer expectations the agent didn't model.

name: Slide Statements

human.symptom: A function where related statements are scattered with interleaved unrelated work — assignments to logically-coupled variables separated by lines that don't share their concern.
human.goal: Related statements sit next to each other; the function reads as a sequence of cohesive sub-steps that are easy to extract.
human.pressure: Reader must hold partial sub-step state in working memory across unrelated statements; the implicit grouping inside the function stays implicit and obstructs further refactoring.
human.tradeoff: Reordering can change behavior if statements aren't actually independent — verify side effects and dependencies before sliding.
human.relief: Setup for Extract Function becomes trivial; the implicit grouping inside the function becomes explicit.
human.trap: Reordering statements without verifying independence — sliding past a statement with hidden side effects (logging that observes state, time-sensitive read) silently changes behavior.

agent.symptom: A function whose related statements are interleaved with unrelated work; the agent reasoning about any sub-step must track state across non-adjacent lines.
agent.goal: Related statements sit next to each other; the agent reads the function as a sequence of cohesive blocks ready for extraction.
agent.pressure: The agent holds partial sub-step state across non-adjacent lines; reasoning about any single concern requires tracking the others through the interleave.
agent.tradeoff: Sliding can silently change behavior if statements aren't truly independent (hidden side effects, timing dependencies, observer effects); the agent verifying the slide must confirm independence at every gap.
agent.relief: The function reads as cohesive blocks the agent can extract or reason about as units; setup for further refactoring becomes mechanical.
agent.trap: Aggressive sliding without verifying side-effect ordering — observer logs, time reads, async dispatch — silently changes behavior the agent's local tests may not catch.

name: Split Loop
after:
const totalSalary = people.reduce((s, p) => s + p.salary, 0);
const youngest    = Math.min(...people.map(p => p.age));

human.symptom: A single loop iterating one collection but doing multiple unrelated jobs — accumulating a sum, finding a minimum, building a derived list, all interwoven in the loop body.
human.goal: Each loop does one thing; mixed-purpose loops separate into named single-purpose passes.
human.pressure: Each line of the body could touch any of the loop's concerns; reasoning about one purpose requires holding all of them; bugs hide where concerns share an iteration variable.
human.tradeoff: Two loops over the same collection are slower than one — only split when the doubled cost is dwarfed by the readability gain (which it usually is).
human.relief: Each loop can then be replaced by a pipeline or extracted by name; bugs concentrate in one purpose at a time.
human.trap: Splitting a loop whose concerns genuinely share state — running total AND previous value, where each iteration depends on the previous — fragments coupled logic into pieces that have to re-derive shared state.

agent.symptom: A single loop body that mixes filter, map, reduce, and side-effect concerns; the agent verifying any change must trace all concerns through the same iteration.
agent.goal: Each loop does one thing; the agent reasons about one concern per loop and can replace each loop independently with a pipeline.
agent.pressure: The agent's per-line reasoning must account for every concern the loop body addresses; changing one concern risks silent interaction with the others.
agent.tradeoff: Two loops over the same collection cost more per iteration than one; for hot paths the runtime overhead matters and the agent verifying performance must measure.
agent.relief: Each loop becomes an independently-replaceable unit (pipeline candidate); the agent's edit surface per concern shrinks.
agent.trap: Splitting loops whose concerns share per-iteration state — accumulator-of-running-difference, look-behind logic — fragments coupled state the agent must now re-derive in each split.

name: Replace Loop with Pipeline

human.symptom: Imperative for/while loops where filter, map, and reduce concerns are mixed by hand — the reader must mentally execute the body to learn what's being produced.
human.goal: Filter / map / reduce expresses the transformation as a sequence of named operations; intent jumps off the page.
human.pressure: Off-by-one errors and accumulator bugs hide in the body and only surface at test time; intent is buried under the mechanism.
human.tradeoff: Pipelines add a tiny per-element function-call overhead — usually negligible, but profile if you're in a hot path.
human.relief: Off-by-one and accumulator bugs vanish; each step is independently testable.
human.trap: Forcing every loop into a pipeline — including ones with early-exit, side-effect accumulators, or genuinely sequential dependencies — produces twisted .reduce() bodies harder to read than the original.

agent.symptom: Imperative for/while loops where the agent must mentally execute the body to learn the result; the loop's purpose isn't readable from its shape.
agent.goal: Transformations read as named operation sequences (filter, map, reduce); the agent recognizes the shape without simulating the loop.
agent.pressure: The agent must trace the loop body step by step to verify behavior; off-by-one bugs hide where the agent's mental simulation diverges from runtime.
agent.tradeoff: Pipeline form adds per-element call overhead and forces the agent to track intermediate collection types through the chain; for hot paths the runtime cost matters.
agent.relief: Intent is readable; the agent reasons about each pipeline stage independently with type signatures documenting the transformation.
agent.trap: Forcing every loop into a pipeline, including ones with early-exit, side-effects, or sequential dependencies, produces .reduce() bodies whose accumulator state the agent has to simulate at every read; the simulation cost exceeds what the original loop's straight-line control flow required.

name: Remove Dead Code
before:
function legacyDiscount(order) { /* unused since 2018 */ }
function modernDiscount(order) { /* the real one */ }
after: function discount(order) { /* the real one */ }

human.symptom: Functions, branches, fields, or imports that no static analysis or human reader can reach — last commented out, last touched years ago, or referenced only by code that itself was removed.
human.goal: Every line in the codebase is reachable and used; readers don't waste cycles on phantom branches.
human.pressure: Readers spend cycles understanding code that never runs; debuggers stop in places that look meaningful but aren't; refactoring proposals have to consider phantom users.
human.tradeoff: You give up the option to revive without a git dive — and 'dead' under static analysis can still be reachable via reflection, dynamic dispatch, or external callers.
human.relief: Smaller surface, faster reading, fewer false leads when debugging.
human.trap: Deleting code that looks dead but is reached via reflection, dynamic dispatch, external callers, or test fixtures — the cleanup ships a regression because static analysis lied.

agent.symptom: The agent finds code (functions, branches, fields) with no inbound references the type system or grep can locate; reasoning about reachability requires assuming static analysis is complete.
agent.goal: Every definition the agent encounters is reachable; reasoning about behavior doesn't have to consider phantom paths.
agent.pressure: The agent's plan-and-execute loop has to consider dead branches as live until proven otherwise; tests pass while code-walking analyses include dead surface area.
agent.tradeoff: Deletion is one-way under static analysis but reachability can hide in reflection, dynamic dispatch, external callers, or runtime config — the agent that deletes without checking risks a regression nothing catches.
agent.relief: The agent's reasoning context shrinks; static analysis becomes ground truth; planning loops don't waste cycles on phantom paths.
agent.trap: Aggressive deletion based purely on grep/static-analysis evidence misses reflection-reachable, plugin-loaded, or externally-referenced code — the cleanup ships a silent regression the agent's tests don't catch.

name: Split Variable

human.symptom: A single variable (often named `temp`, `result`, `value`) reassigned multiple times to hold conceptually distinct values — perimeter, then area; current iteration result, then accumulator.
human.goal: Each variable has one role; reassignment patterns reflect distinct purposes rather than reused storage.
human.pressure: The reader must track which role the variable currently holds; bugs hide where one role's update accidentally clobbers another; refactoring either use is impossible without disentangling.
human.tradeoff: If the two uses were actually coupled — shared init or synchronized update — splitting them invites drift the single mutation kept in sync.
human.relief: Names match purpose; the type system can narrow each role; refactoring each use becomes local.
human.trap: Splitting variables whose uses were genuinely coupled — accumulator that depends on a previous-iteration version of itself — fragments coherent state into separate variables that have to re-establish the coupling.

agent.symptom: The agent finds a variable reassigned with values of conceptually different types or domains; reasoning about any expression involving it requires knowing which role is currently active.
agent.goal: Each variable holds one role with a stable name; the agent reasons about names without tracking reassignment timeline.
agent.pressure: The agent must trace through reassignments to know what any reference currently means; type-narrowing in unions becomes guesswork at every read site.
agent.tradeoff: If the two uses were actually coupled (shared init, synchronized update), splitting forces the agent to re-derive the coupling across two variables.
agent.relief: The agent reasons about each variable as a stable name; the type system can narrow each role; each use becomes independently refactorable.
agent.trap: Splitting variables whose uses genuinely shared state forces the agent to re-establish the coupling outside the variable, complicating the original logic.

name: Rename Field

human.symptom: A class field whose name is ambiguous (`name` on a Position class — role name or person?), shadowed by language keywords, or describes implementation type rather than domain role.
human.goal: Field names match the domain role they play; readers don't need to inspect usage to know what a field means.
human.pressure: Every reader/writer of the class must figure out what the field means from context; bugs surface when readers assume the wrong meaning.
human.tradeoff: Same drift as Rename Variable, amplified across the field's read/write surface and any persistence shadows (DB columns, JSON schemas, APIs).
human.relief: Stronger encapsulation; future-you reads the class definition and immediately understands its shape.
human.trap: Renaming a field without updating the persistence shadow — DB columns, JSON schema, API responses still use the old name and break serialization/deserialization silently.

agent.symptom: A field whose name does not match its role in the domain; every read or write site forces the agent to load the class definition to recover what the field represents before reasoning about the access.
agent.goal: Field names carry the domain term; read or write sites resolve to one token of name without loading the class definition for context recovery.
agent.pressure: Every access site pays the cost of loading the class definition to recover what the field stores; tokens consumed scale with the number of consumers, and generated code that misinterprets the field's role ships against the wrong invariant.
agent.tradeoff: Renaming a field invalidates more cached associations than a variable rename — persistence layers (DB columns, JSON schemas, API contracts) carry the old name until they update.
agent.relief: The agent reasons about field access with the field's name as ground truth; consumer-side reasoning becomes self-documenting.
agent.trap: Renaming a field whose current name another reviewer would have accepted forces coordinated migrations across every external surface (database columns, JSON schemas, API contracts) without changing what the field stores.

name: Replace Derived Variable with Query

human.symptom: A field that mirrors values computed from other fields, updated by hand at multiple write sites — `total` updated every time `items` changes.
human.goal: Values computed from other state are computed on demand; no separate field needs to be kept in sync.
human.pressure: The derived field can drift from its source; every writer of the underlying field must remember to update the derived one; bugs are 'why is total wrong here?' instead of local.
human.tradeoff: If the derivation is expensive and the source rarely changes, recomputing on every read may be wasteful — measure before deciding.
human.relief: Mutation scope shrinks; reasoning about state is simpler; no chance of the derived field drifting from its source.
human.trap: Replacing every derived value with a query — even ones that wrap an expensive computation called many times per render — substitutes correctness for runtime cost that matters.

agent.symptom: The agent finds a field whose value mirrors a computation on other fields; every writer of the source field must update the derived field consistently or the values drift.
agent.goal: Derived values are computed on demand; the agent reasons about state by reading source fields and trusting derivations.
agent.pressure: The agent must trace every writer of the source field to verify the derived field stays in sync; bugs hide where one writer forgot to update the derivation.
agent.tradeoff: Recomputing on every read can multiply cost if the derivation is expensive and the source rarely changes; the agent verifying performance must measure before deciding.
agent.relief: Mutation scope shrinks to source fields; the agent reasons about state without modeling derivation update timing; consistency is by construction.
agent.trap: Replacing every derived field with a query — including ones wrapping expensive computations called many times — trades runtime cost for correctness without measuring the impact.

name: Decompose Conditional

human.symptom: Multi-clause conditionals whose meaning isn't obvious from the expression — `if (date.getMonth() >= 5 && date.getMonth() <= 8)` instead of `if (isSummer(date))`.
human.goal: Conditions and their consequents read as named domain decisions: isInSummer(), discountFor(date), etc.
human.pressure: Readers parse the expression every time; comments accumulate to explain what it means; debugging requires evaluating the expression mentally.
human.tradeoff: Names that aren't crisper than the underlying condition add ceremony — only extract when the named function/variable says something the condition can't.
human.relief: The branching logic reads top-to-bottom as a story; bugs concentrate in the named pieces.
human.trap: Extracting names that aren't crisper than the underlying condition — adds a layer of indirection without revealing intent.

agent.symptom: Multi-clause conditional expressions whose domain meaning isn't readable from the syntax; the agent must parse the expression every time it encounters it.
agent.goal: Conditions read as named domain decisions; the agent reasons about isSummer(date) instead of re-deriving the month range.
agent.pressure: The agent re-parses the expression at every reference; debugging the condition's value requires the agent to mentally evaluate the full chain.
agent.tradeoff: Extracted names that aren't crisper than the original condition add a layer of indirection — the agent now follows a name to find the same expression.
agent.relief: The agent reasons about named domain decisions; the branching logic reads top-to-bottom as a story.
agent.trap: Extracting names that don't sharpen the condition — `isMonthBetweenFiveAndEight` instead of `isSummer` — adds indirection without revealing intent.

name: Consolidate Conditional Expression
after: if (isIneligibleForBonus(employee)) return 0;

human.symptom: Multiple conditions in sequence (or chained) leading to the same action — three guard clauses each returning 0, or three branches each running the same handler.
human.goal: Multiple conditions leading to the same action collapse into one named predicate.
human.pressure: The shared rationale is invisible; adding a new condition with the same effect means touching N places; bugs hide where one of the branches diverges accidentally.
human.tradeoff: Combining conditions can hide their independent reasons — only consolidate when they truly express the same business rule.
human.relief: The shared rationale becomes visible and namable; new conditions extend one place instead of N.
human.trap: Combining conditions that look the same but encode independent reasons — the consolidated predicate hides distinct rules that need to evolve separately.

agent.symptom: Multiple conditions in sequence lead to the same action; the agent must verify each branch leads to identical behavior and that adding a new condition won't accidentally diverge.
agent.goal: The conditions collapse into one named predicate; the agent reasons about one rule with one action.
agent.pressure: Adding or modifying any branch's behavior requires the agent to update every branch consistently; the shared rationale is invisible.
agent.tradeoff: If the conditions encode independent reasons (different rules that happen to produce the same outcome today), collapsing them hides distinctions the agent will need to re-split later.
agent.relief: The agent reasons about one named predicate with one consequent; new conditions extend in one place.
agent.trap: Collapsing conditions that look the same but encode independent rules hides distinctions the agent will need to re-split when one rule evolves differently from the others.

name: Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses

human.symptom: Functions with deeply nested if/else where the happy path is buried inside multiple levels of indentation, and edge cases are conditionals around the main flow.
human.goal: Edge cases bail out early at the top of the function; the main flow is unindented and tells the happy path linearly.
human.pressure: The dominant case is hidden under indentation; readers must trace down through edge-case branches to find the main flow; new edge cases extend an already-tangled structure.
human.tradeoff: If multiple paths share work, premature returns can duplicate that work — extract first, then guard.
human.relief: Indentation drops; the dominant case is obvious; new edge cases land at the top without disturbing the rest.
human.trap: Inlining guard clauses for every condition — including ones where the edge case shares work with the main path; the early returns duplicate work the structure was sharing.

agent.symptom: A function with deeply nested if/else where the happy path is buried under indentation; the agent must trace through edge-case branches to find the main flow.
agent.goal: Edge cases bail out early; the main flow is unindented and reads linearly as the dominant story.
agent.pressure: The agent's parsing of the function's intent is obscured by indentation; reasoning about the happy path requires tracking which edge cases have already been ruled out.
agent.tradeoff: Early returns can duplicate work if multiple paths share follow-up logic; the agent inlining guards must verify the shared work is genuinely separable.
agent.relief: The agent reads the happy path linearly with edge cases as exceptions; new edge cases land at the top without disturbing the main flow.
agent.trap: Inlining guards for every condition — including ones that shared follow-up work — fragments the shared logic across early-return branches the agent must keep consistent.

name: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
after: event.handle(); // ClickEvent and KeyEvent each implement handle()

human.symptom: The same switch (or if/else chain) over a type code appears in multiple places — adding a new case means hunting them all down.
human.goal: Each case becomes a class implementing a shared interface; dispatch happens once via virtual call.
human.pressure: Dispatch logic duplicates across files; new cases are easy to miss; the type-code coupling amplifies with every additional consumer.
human.tradeoff: If only one switch on the type code exists, polymorphism is overkill — wait for the second or third repeat before extracting subclasses.
human.relief: Adding a new case is one new class; the type system tells you what's missing.
human.trap: Polymorphism worship — a switch with two stable cases becomes a class hierarchy of two trivial subclasses, paying class-hierarchy overhead with no flexibility return.

agent.symptom: A switch on a type code that appears in multiple files; the agent adding a new case must grep for every site and update each consistently or risk silent inconsistency.
agent.goal: Each case is a class implementing a shared interface; the agent adds a new case by adding one class, and the type system tells it what's still missing.
agent.pressure: Dispatch logic duplicates across files; the agent must enumerate and update every switch on every addition, with no compile-time check that the set is complete.
agent.tradeoff: Polymorphic dispatch is implicit at call sites — the agent can no longer see the full set of branches in one place and must enumerate subclasses across files to reason about behavior.
agent.relief: Adding a new variant is mechanical and the type checker enforces completeness; the agent's plan-and-execute loop for new cases is bounded.
agent.trap: Replacing every switch with polymorphism — including ones with two stable cases — creates a class hierarchy the agent must navigate without buying any extension flexibility.

name: Introduce Special Case
before: const name = customer === 'unknown' ? 'occupant' : customer.name;
after: const name = customer.name; // UnknownCustomer.name returns 'occupant'

human.symptom: The same null-or-special check repeats across multiple consumers — `customer === 'unknown' ? 'occupant' : customer.name` scattered across files.
human.goal: A repeating null-or-special check becomes a Null Object (or Special Case) that responds sensibly to the same interface.
human.pressure: Every consumer must remember the check; behavior for the special case drifts as consumers diverge; bugs hide where one consumer forgot the check.
human.tradeoff: Adds a tiny class for one case; only worthwhile when the special case appears in 2+ consumers.
human.relief: Callers stop branching on identity; the special behavior lives in one place.
human.trap: Adding a Null Object (or Special Case) class for a special check used in only one place — creates a class for a one-off conditional.

agent.symptom: The agent finds the same null-or-special check repeating across multiple consumers; consistency depends on every consumer remembering the pattern.
agent.goal: The special case responds to the same interface as the real case; the agent reasons without branching at every call site.
agent.pressure: Every consumer is a chance to miss the check; the agent verifying consistency must audit every site.
agent.tradeoff: Adding a Null Object class for a special case used in only one place creates ceremony around what was a one-line check; the agent now loads a class to handle one branch.
agent.relief: The agent reasons polymorphically; the special behavior lives in one class and consumers don't branch.
agent.trap: Introducing a Null Object class for special checks used in only one place creates a class the agent must load and reason about with no consistency gain.

name: Introduce Assertion
before:
// rate must be positive
const tax = base * rate;
after:
if (rate <= 0) throw new Error('rate must be positive');
const tax = base * rate;

human.symptom: Code that depends on unwritten invariants — `const tax = base * rate;` that assumes rate > 0, with no enforcement and only a stale comment if any.
human.goal: Invariants the code assumes are stated explicitly; readers don't need to deduce them.
human.pressure: Bugs that violate the invariant bubble out as mysterious downstream errors; readers must reconstruct the invariant from context; the assumption drifts silently as the code evolves.
human.tradeoff: Assertions used as control flow couple production behavior to debug-mode invariants — keep them as runtime contracts that should never fire.
human.relief: Bugs that violate the invariant fail loudly at the source instead of bubbling out as mysterious downstream errors.
human.trap: Using assertions as control flow — production code that depends on the assertion firing or not firing becomes coupled to debug-mode behavior.

agent.symptom: Code that depends on unwritten invariants the agent must reconstruct from context; bugs that violate the invariant surface far from the source.
agent.goal: Invariants are stated explicitly; the agent reads them and reasons about behavior under their guarantee.
agent.pressure: The agent must reconstruct invariants from surrounding code; bugs surface far from the source and tracing them costs reasoning hops.
agent.tradeoff: Assertions used as control flow couple production behavior to debug-mode invariants; the agent that conflates the two ships a flow-dependent change disguised as documentation.
agent.relief: Invariants fail loudly at the source; the agent's debugging traces are short; assumptions become enforceable contracts.
agent.trap: Coupling production behavior to assertion presence/absence — the agent reads them as documentation but the runtime depends on them firing or not.

name: Separate Query from Modifier

human.symptom: A function that both returns a value AND mutates state — `findMiscreant(people)` that returns the miscreant AND alerts them.
human.goal: Functions either return a value or mutate state, never both — callers can compose them without surprise.
human.pressure: Callers can't query without triggering the side effect; tests must work around the dual contract; reasoning about side effects becomes non-local.
human.tradeoff: If the modification and the query truly cannot be separated (e.g. find-and-remove on a queue), the constraint is fundamental — leave the combined operation but document it.
human.relief: Reasoning about side effects is local; tests target each shape independently.
human.trap: Splitting a function whose query and modification truly cannot be separated — find-and-remove on a queue, atomic compare-and-swap — fragments operations that need atomicity.

agent.symptom: A function the agent calls for a query also mutates state; the agent reasoning about safety must trace the mutation across consumers.
agent.goal: Functions either return or mutate, never both; the agent composes queries without surprise side effects.
agent.pressure: Every call to the function pays for both contracts; the agent can't query without triggering mutation, which complicates testing and composition.
agent.tradeoff: If the modification and query are genuinely atomic (find-and-remove, compare-and-swap), splitting them introduces a race window the agent must close at every call site.
agent.relief: The agent reasons about side effects locally; queries compose cleanly; tests target each shape independently.
agent.trap: Splitting atomic query-and-modify operations introduces race windows the agent must reason about at every call site — the cure becomes worse than the smell.

name: Parameterize Function
before:
function tenPercentRaise(person)  { person.salary *= 1.10; }
function fivePercentRaise(person) { person.salary *= 1.05; }
after: function raise(person, factor) { person.salary *= 1 + factor; }

human.symptom: Two or more near-identical functions that differ only in literal values — `tenPercentRaise(person)` and `fivePercentRaise(person)` differ only in 1.10 vs 1.05.
human.goal: Two near-identical functions that differ only in literal values combine into one with a parameter.
human.pressure: Bug fixes must land in every variant; new variants are new functions; the shared shape isn't expressed anywhere.
human.tradeoff: If the variations are conceptually different operations, one parameterized function will accumulate flags and special cases — keep them separate then.
human.relief: One canonical implementation; new variations are new parameter values, not new functions.
human.trap: Parameterizing functions whose variations are conceptually different operations — the parameterized function accumulates flags and special cases that overwhelm the original simplicity.

agent.symptom: The agent finds near-identical functions differing only in literal values; consistency depends on every variant staying in sync.
agent.goal: One canonical function with a parameter; the agent reasons about one body and verifies parameter values at call sites.
agent.pressure: Bug fixes must land in every variant; the agent must find and update each consistently or risk drift.
agent.tradeoff: If the variations encode conceptually different operations, the parameterized function grows flags and special cases the agent must thread through — worse than the original duplication.
agent.relief: One canonical implementation the agent reasons about; new variations are new parameter values, not new code paths.
agent.trap: Parameterizing conceptually different operations accumulates flag-driven branches the agent must reason about — the function becomes a switch statement in disguise.

name: Remove Flag Argument
after:
function setHeight(value) { /* ... */ }
function setWidth(value)  { /* ... */ }

human.symptom: A function with a boolean (or enum) flag parameter that dispatches to different internal behaviors — `setDimension('height', value)` vs `setDimension('width', value)`.
human.goal: Each flag value becomes its own well-named function; callers say what they mean rather than passing booleans.
human.pressure: Call sites must remember the flag's meaning; the function's body is a switch the agent reads through to find each branch; new flag values touch one body that handles many concerns.
human.tradeoff: Two replacement functions with similar bodies introduce duplication — pair this with Extract Function for shared internals.
human.relief: Call sites read fluently; new variations land as new functions instead of new switch cases.
human.trap: Splitting flag-dispatched functions whose branches are mostly shared body — produces N functions with N copies of the same body, inverting the original abstraction.

agent.symptom: A function with a flag parameter that dispatches to different internal behaviors; the agent must trace the flag's value through the body to verify which branch any call exercises.
agent.goal: Each flag value becomes a named function; the agent reads call sites as direct invocations of the intended behavior.
agent.pressure: The agent must reason about flag values at every call site; the function's body conflates multiple concerns the agent must mentally split.
agent.tradeoff: If the branches share substantial body, splitting produces duplication the agent must keep in sync; pair this with Extract Function for shared internals.
agent.relief: Call sites read fluently; the agent reasons about one function per concern.
agent.trap: Splitting flag-dispatched functions without extracting shared body creates N copies of the same logic the agent must keep in sync — the cure becomes the duplication smell.

name: Preserve Whole Object
before: if (room.lowTemp < range.low || room.highTemp > range.high) { /* ... */ }
after: if (range.includes(room)) { /* ... */ }

human.symptom: A function call that pulls several fields out of an object to pass them in — `f(room.lowTemp, room.highTemp, room.humidity)` instead of `f(room)`.
human.goal: Instead of pulling several values out of an object to pass them in, pass the object itself.
human.pressure: Adding a new field that the function needs touches every call site; the function's contract is verbose and shifts every time it grows.
human.tradeoff: Passing the whole object adds coupling to its full surface — only do this when the called function might reasonably need other parts of the object.
human.relief: Signatures shrink; adding a needed field is internal; consumers don't have to plumb new arguments through.
human.trap: Passing whole objects when the function only needs one field — introduces unnecessary coupling to the object's full surface.

agent.symptom: The agent sees call sites unpacking multiple fields from an object to pass to a function; adding any field the function later needs touches every call site.
agent.goal: The function takes the object; the agent updates one place when the function needs new fields.
agent.pressure: Every call site is a coordination point; the agent verifying a signature change must update every unpacking explicitly.
agent.tradeoff: Passing the whole object couples the function to the object's full surface; the agent reasoning about the function must consider what other fields it might quietly read.
agent.relief: Signatures shrink; adding a needed field is an internal change; the agent reasons about one parameter at every call.
agent.trap: Passing whole objects when only one field is needed couples the function to the object's full surface the agent must consider as the function's input scope.

name: Replace Parameter with Query
after: const final = discounted(order); // computes basePrice and level itself

human.symptom: A function that takes a parameter the caller computed from data already available to the function — `discounted(order, basePrice, level)` where the function can compute basePrice and level itself.
human.goal: When a function can compute its own answer from already-available state, callers don't have to pre-compute it.
human.pressure: Every caller pays the homework cost; signatures inflate with values the function can derive; the duplication of derivation logic scatters.
human.tradeoff: If the query has side effects or is expensive, passing the value is genuinely better — only replace when the query is pure and cheap.
human.relief: Signatures shrink; consumers stop doing the function's homework.
human.trap: Replacing parameters with queries when the query is expensive or has side effects — multiplies cost and introduces hidden coupling.

agent.symptom: A function takes parameters its callers computed from data the function already has access to; the agent verifying any call must reproduce the caller's computation.
agent.goal: The function computes its own answer; the agent calls it without pre-computing the inputs.
agent.pressure: Every caller pays the homework cost; the duplication of derivation logic scatters and the agent must keep callers in sync with the function's expectations.
agent.tradeoff: If the query is expensive or has side effects, replacing the parameter multiplies cost or introduces hidden coupling the agent must reason about.
agent.relief: Signatures shrink; the agent calls the function directly without reproducing caller-side derivations.
agent.trap: Replacing parameters with queries that are expensive or have side effects multiplies cost or introduces hidden coupling the agent reads as 'just a parameter swap'.

name: Replace Constructor with Factory Function
before: const employee = new Employee(name, 'engineer', salary);

human.symptom: Object creation directly via `new Class(...)` where the construction logic needs validation, subclass selection, or instance caching but the constructor can't express any of it.
human.goal: Object creation goes through a named function that can validate, choose subclasses, or return cached instances.
human.pressure: Constructors can't validate, return subclasses, or cache; consumers either accept the limitation or scatter pre-construction logic at every call site.
human.tradeoff: Hides the actual class from callers — make sure your factory's name still expresses the produced shape clearly.
human.relief: Construction can vary per case; consumers don't depend on which concrete class they're getting.
human.trap: Wrapping every constructor in a factory function for principle — adds a layer of indirection without buying validation, polymorphism, or caching capability.

agent.symptom: The agent finds constructors used directly where construction needs validation, subclass selection, or caching — none of which constructors can express.
agent.goal: Construction goes through a named factory the agent can extend with validation, polymorphism, or caching as one location.
agent.pressure: The agent's reasoning about construction must consider pre-construction logic scattered at every call site; constructors hide the capability for the patterns the code actually needs.
agent.tradeoff: The factory hides the actual class from callers; the agent must ensure the factory's name still expresses the produced shape clearly or call sites become opaque.
agent.relief: The agent extends construction in one place; consumers don't depend on which concrete class they're getting.
agent.trap: Wrapping every constructor in a factory adds an indirection layer the agent must navigate without buying any new construction capability.

name: Pull Up Method
before:
class Manager  extends Employee { name() { return this._name; } }
class Engineer extends Employee { name() { return this._name; } }

human.symptom: Two or more subclasses implement the same method identically — `Manager.name()` and `Engineer.name()` both return `this._name` with no variation.
human.goal: Methods that subclasses implement identically move to the shared superclass.
human.pressure: Bug fixes must land in every copy; the shared behavior isn't expressed in the hierarchy; new subclasses copy the same boilerplate.
human.tradeoff: If the methods only superficially resemble each other, pulling up creates a fake-shared abstraction — unify only when behavior is actually identical.
human.relief: One implementation, one place to fix; subclasses focus on what's actually different.
human.trap: Pulling up methods that only superficially resemble each other — the parent gets a method whose subclasses each interpret differently, creating a fake-shared abstraction.

agent.symptom: Two or more subclasses implement the same method identically; the agent verifying behavior must check every subclass and confirm they actually agree.
agent.goal: The method lives on the parent with one implementation; queries about behavior across subclasses load one method body instead of paying the token cost of loading N near-identical bodies.
agent.pressure: Bug fixes must land in every copy; the agent verifying consistency must update every subclass and risk drift.
agent.tradeoff: If the methods only superficially resemble each other (same name, different semantics), pulling up creates a fake-shared abstraction the agent must constantly disambiguate.
agent.relief: Edits to the shared behavior land in one parent method; the agent does not load N subclass bodies to verify they still agree, and generated code that calls the method from any subclass dispatches to the same implementation.
agent.trap: Pulling up methods that share a name but not behavior produces one parent method the agent reads as canonical; generated code that calls the method from any subclass runs the parent's behavior, dropping the subclass-specific work the original separate methods performed.

name: Push Down Method

human.symptom: A method on the parent class used by only one subclass — `Employee.quota()` used only by `Salesperson`.
human.goal: Methods used by only one subclass live with that subclass, not on the shared superclass.
human.pressure: Every other subclass carries surface it doesn't use; readers can't tell which methods are shared and which are subclass-specific; the parent's true interface is muddied.
human.tradeoff: If the method is occasionally needed in the parent, pushing it down forces awkward type checks back at consumers — verify usage first.
human.relief: The superclass surface shrinks; subclasses that don't need the method aren't burdened by it.
human.trap: Pushing down methods used occasionally in the parent for type checks or polymorphic calls — forces awkward downcasts back at the parent's consumers.

agent.symptom: A method declared on the parent that only one subclass overrides or invokes; the parent's interface includes a method that does not apply to most instances the agent reasons about.
agent.goal: The method lives on the subclass that uses it; reading the parent's interface returns only the methods every instance supports, dropping the irrelevant declaration from the agent's window.
agent.pressure: The parent's interface is muddied with subclass-specific methods; the agent can't tell which methods apply to which subclass without inspecting usage.
agent.tradeoff: If the parent occasionally consults the method for type checks or polymorphic dispatch, pushing it down forces awkward downcasts at every consumer the agent must verify.
agent.relief: The parent's interface shrinks by one method; queries about any subclass's behavior load fewer irrelevant declarations into the window, and code generated against the parent's interface no longer references a method most instances do not support.
agent.trap: Pushing down a method that callers reach through a parent-typed reference forces every such call site to downcast first; each downcast is a runtime type check the agent's generated code has to handle at every consumer.

name: Replace Type Code with Subclasses

human.symptom: A class with a `kind` or `type` field (string or enum) plus methods that switch on it — `Employee` carrying a `type` field used to dispatch `bonus()` to different formulas.
human.goal: A 'kind' string field becomes a real subclass type; the type system enforces the legal set.
human.pressure: Every method that varies by type must switch; the compiler can't enforce that all kinds are handled; new kinds require updating every switch.
human.tradeoff: If only one or two switches exist on the type code, subclassing is over-design; combine with Replace Conditional with Polymorphism only when dispatch repeats.
human.relief: Compile-time checks that no kind is missed; per-kind behavior lives where it belongs.
human.trap: Replacing the type code with subclasses when only one or two switches exist on it — over-design for a coordination point that's barely a smell.

agent.symptom: A class with a kind field plus methods that switch on it; the agent adding a new kind must find every switch and update each consistently.
agent.goal: Each kind is a subclass; the agent adds a new kind by adding one class, and the type system tells it what's still missing.
agent.pressure: The agent must enumerate every switch on every addition; the type system can't enforce completeness so the agent verifies by grep.
agent.tradeoff: If only one or two switches exist on the type code, the subclass hierarchy is over-design; the agent now navigates a class tree for what was a single switch.
agent.relief: Adding a new kind is mechanical and type-system-enforced; the agent's plan-and-execute loop for new variants is bounded.
agent.trap: Subclassing for type codes used in only one or two switches creates a hierarchy the agent must navigate for a coordination cost that was already small.

name: Extract Superclass
before:
class Employee   { name; id; salary; }
class Department { name; id; budget; }

human.symptom: Two classes with substantial shared structure — `Employee` and `Department` both carrying `name`, `id`, and similar id-management methods.
human.goal: Two classes with substantial shared structure get a common parent that owns the shared bits.
human.pressure: Bug fixes must land in both; future shared behavior has no obvious home; the relationship between the classes is invisible to readers.
human.tradeoff: Inheritance is inflexible — if the duplication is shallow, prefer Extract Class (composition) over Extract Superclass.
human.relief: Bug fixes and new shared behavior land in one place; the relationship between the classes is documented in code.
human.trap: Extracting a superclass for shallow duplication — inheritance is inflexible, and the parent becomes a constraint on future divergence that composition (Extract Class) would have avoided.

agent.symptom: Two classes with substantial shared structure (fields, methods); the agent verifying changes must update both consistently.
agent.goal: The shared structure lives in a common parent; the agent reasons about shared behavior in one place.
agent.pressure: Bug fixes must land in both classes; the agent's reasoning about shared invariants must verify they hold identically across both.
agent.tradeoff: Inheritance is inflexible; for shallow duplication, the agent's downstream changes are constrained by the parent in ways composition (Extract Class) would have avoided.
agent.relief: Shared behavior lives in one place; the agent's reasoning about the relationship is documented in code via the inheritance link.
agent.trap: Extracting superclasses for shallow duplication locks the agent into inheritance constraints when composition would have left both classes free to diverge.

name: Collapse Hierarchy
before:
class Employee {}
class FullTimeEmployee extends Employee {}
after: class Employee {}

human.symptom: A subclass that no longer differs meaningfully from its parent — an empty subclass, or one that overrides nothing the parent didn't already do.
human.goal: A subclass that no longer differs meaningfully from its parent merges back in.
human.pressure: Readers navigate a hierarchy that adds no value; ceremony around construction and dispatch persists; future maintenance must touch both classes for any change.
human.tradeoff: Collapsing too eagerly destroys an extension point you'll later want — only collapse when the variant has been zero-sum for a sustained period.
human.relief: Smaller hierarchy, less ceremony, fewer files to navigate.
human.trap: Collapsing a hierarchy whose subclass is currently quiet but documents a real future variation — destroys an extension point you'll need to re-introduce later at higher cost.

agent.symptom: A subclass that no longer differs meaningfully from its parent; the agent navigating the hierarchy traverses indirection for no behavioral variation.
agent.goal: The subclass folds into the parent; the agent reads one class instead of a degenerate two-class hierarchy.
agent.pressure: The agent's reasoning pays the hierarchy ceremony cost on every reference; future maintenance touches both classes for any change.
agent.tradeoff: If the subclass documents a future variation (extension point, planned divergence), collapsing destroys it; the agent that collapses without checking forecloses options.
agent.relief: Smaller hierarchy; less ceremony; the agent loads one class instead of navigating a degenerate two-class chain.
agent.trap: Collapsing subclasses that document planned future variation destroys extension points the agent will need to re-introduce later at higher cost.

name: Replace Subclass with Delegate

human.symptom: A subclass that overrides several methods to implement variant behavior — `PremiumBooking extends Booking` overriding `charge()`, `discount()`, `notify()` with premium variants.
human.goal: Behavior that varied via inheritance now varies via a delegate object that implements the variant interface.
human.pressure: Behavior can't change at runtime; combining variants requires multiple inheritance; the inheritance relationship may violate Liskov in subtle ways.
human.tradeoff: Composition is more verbose at construction sites — accept the verbosity in exchange for the flexibility.
human.relief: Variants can be combined or swapped at runtime; Liskov violations vanish; the hierarchy tree flattens.
human.trap: Replacing every subclass with composition — including ones where the inheritance contract genuinely holds — pays construction-site verbosity for no real fit improvement.

agent.symptom: A subclass that overrides several methods to implement variant behavior; the agent reasoning about polymorphic dispatch must enumerate variants across the hierarchy.
agent.goal: Variants live in delegate objects the host holds and forwards to; the agent reads one host class plus the held delegate's interface instead of climbing an inheritance chain to predict behavior.
agent.pressure: Behavior can't change at runtime; combining variants requires multiple inheritance the agent must work around; Liskov violations hide in override behavior.
agent.tradeoff: Composition is more verbose at construction sites; the agent loses syntactic polymorphism and must verify behavior through explicit delegation calls.
agent.relief: Behavior changes at runtime by swapping the delegate; the agent reasons against one host signature plus the delegate's interface, without loading the inheritance graph to verify which override applies to a given instance.
agent.trap: Replacing inheritance with delegation on hierarchies where every subclass honors the parent's contract adds construction-site setup and a forwarding method per parent method without changing what the agent's generated calls do.

name: Extract Class

human.symptom: A class with multiple cohesive sub-concepts inside it — Person carrying officeAreaCode + officeNumber + telephoneNumber() method, where Phone is hiding.
human.goal: A cohesive sub-concept inside a class becomes its own class with its own name, fields, and methods.
human.pressure: The parent class's surface grows past what one type should own; tests touch unrelated concerns together; changes to one concept risk side effects on another.
human.tradeoff: Premature class extraction adds ceremony — extract when 3+ fields and at least one operation cluster around a single concept that the parent class doesn't own.
human.relief: Each class has one purpose; tests target the small unit; the parent class shrinks.
human.trap: Extracting a class when the candidate concept is just 1-2 fields without behavior — adds a class file with no encapsulation gain.

agent.symptom: A class whose surface mixes multiple cohesive sub-concepts; the agent reasoning about any single concept must skim past the others to find what it needs.
agent.goal: Each class has one purpose; the agent loads a small focused file to reason about any single concept.
agent.pressure: The agent's reasoning context per method inflates with unrelated members; changes to one concept require reasoning about all of them.
agent.tradeoff: Extracting too eagerly — 1-2 fields with no behavior — adds a class file the agent must load with no encapsulation gain.
agent.relief: Smaller focused units; the agent tests one concept at a time and reasons about each class as a coherent whole.
agent.trap: Extracting candidate concepts that are just trivial field groups creates class files the agent must navigate without buying any encapsulation gain.

name: Replace Primitive with Object

human.symptom: Domain concepts (Money, PhoneNumber, OrderId, Currency) represented as raw strings, numbers, or booleans — the type system can't tell two domains apart.
human.goal: Each domain concept has a small typed home — Money, PhoneNumber, OrderId — that knows its rules.
human.pressure: Validation and formatting scatter across every consumer; the wrong primitive in the wrong slot compiles fine and fails at runtime; behavior that belongs with the concept has nowhere to live.
human.tradeoff: Wrapping every primitive is overkill — wrap when the concept needs validation, formatting, or domain-specific behavior beyond what the primitive offers.
human.relief: Misuse becomes a type error; behavior accretes around the concept; refactoring is local to the wrapper.
human.trap: Wrapping every primitive on principle — Name, Title, Description as separate classes whose only methods are toString() — adds typing ceremony without enforcing any domain rule.

agent.symptom: Function signatures use raw strings and numbers where domain concepts hide; the agent cannot tell from the type whether an argument is the right kind of thing.
agent.goal: Each domain concept has its own typed wrapper; the agent's type checker catches wrong-primitive-in-wrong-slot before runtime.
agent.pressure: The agent must inspect call-site context (variable names, surrounding code) to verify a primitive is the right kind; validation and formatting scatter.
agent.tradeoff: Each wrapper is a class the agent must instantiate at every entry point; for primitives without domain rules the wrapper is overhead with no return.
agent.relief: Wrong-primitive misuse becomes a type error the agent catches without runtime testing; behavior accretes around the concept where the agent expects to find it.
agent.trap: Wrapping every primitive — including ones with no domain rules — adds boilerplate the agent must navigate at every signature with no reasoning benefit.

name: Hide Delegate
before: const street = order.customer.address.street;
after:
// inside Order: customerStreet() { return this.customer.address.street; }
const street = order.customerStreet();

human.symptom: Callers use long dotted access paths to walk through one object to reach another's data — `order.customer.address.street` exposes every intermediate boundary.
human.goal: Callers ask the closest object for what they want; the object delegates internally without exposing its collaborators.
human.pressure: Every link in the chain is a coupling point; renaming any intermediate field breaks every caller; consumers depend on the full graph shape.
human.tradeoff: Adds a passthrough method on the parent for every delegated operation — only worth it for operations that are repeated across consumers.
human.relief: Encapsulation tightens; intermediate objects can change shape without breaking callers.
human.trap: Wrapping every dotted access in a passthrough — including chains used only once where the wrapper adds cost without removing real coupling.
